Schools and movements

Psychoanalysis

The unconscious, conflict and personal history.

What does it propose?Much of mental life is unconscious. Desires, conflicts and memories we are not aware of influence what we feel, think and do, and can produce symptoms.
What does it study?Neurotic symptoms, dreams, slips of the tongue, sexuality, child development, defence mechanisms and, later, early relationships.
How does it study it?Case studies in the consulting room: free association, dream interpretation and analysis of transference, that is, of the feelings the patient transfers onto the therapist.
Who took part?Sigmund Freud and Josef Breuer; later Carl Jung, Alfred Adler, Anna Freud, Melanie Klein, Karen Horney, Donald Winnicott, Erik Erikson and John Bowlby, among many others.
What remains?The "talking cure" as the basis of psychotherapy, the importance of childhood and relationships, the notion of defence mechanisms and brief psychodynamic therapies with empirical evaluation.
What is debated?Many of Freud's specific hypotheses have not been confirmed. Critics point to how hard his theories are to test, the use of poorly controlled cases and a view of women typical of his time.

Context

In late nineteenth-century Vienna the neurologist Sigmund Freud (1856–1939) was treating patients with paralysis, blindness or anxiety that had no apparent physical cause. With his colleague Josef Breuer he observed that symptoms improved when patients talked about painful experiences. Between 1895 and 1900 this gave rise to a method of treatment and a general theory of the mind.

Key ideas

  • The unconscious: what we do not know about ourselves influences our behaviour.
  • Id, ego and superego (1923): the drives, the part that adapts to reality and the internalised moral conscience.
  • Defence mechanisms: repression, denial, projection or rationalisation protect against anxiety, sometimes at a high price. Anna Freud systematised them in 1936.
  • Development and relationships: childhood leaves its mark. Later authors such as Klein, Winnicott and Bowlby emphasised relationships with caregivers more than drives.

The branches that emerged

The movement soon split. Jung founded analytical psychology, with the collective unconscious and archetypes. Adler founded individual psychology, centred on feelings of inferiority and social interest. Horney and Erich Fromm stressed culture. In France, Jacques Lacan proposed a rereading based on language, highly influential in Latin America and Spain.

Historical importance and current support

Few theories have influenced twentieth-century culture so much: literature, film, art and everyday language. As science, the record is mixed. Hypotheses such as a universal Oedipus complex have no empirical support. On the other hand, the existence of non-conscious mental processes is well established, though understood differently, and brief psychodynamic therapies have shown in clinical trials an efficacy comparable to other psychotherapies for some problems, such as depression.

Famous cases

Psychoanalysis was built on clinical cases. "Anna O." (Bertha Pappenheim), treated by Josef Breuer, called her treatment "the talking cure". Freud wrote about Dora, Little Hans and the Wolf Man. Later historians pointed out that some of these cases had less favourable outcomes than reported. Bertha Pappenheim, for example, remained ill for some time and later became a leading pioneer of social work in Germany.

From the couch to psychodynamic therapy

Classical analysis involved several sessions a week for years. Today's psychodynamic therapies are usually shorter, face to face and focused on relationship patterns. Some trials, such as those reviewed by Jonathan Shedler (2010) and Falk Leichsenring, find effects comparable to other therapies in depression and some personality disorders, though with fewer studies.

Ideas that entered the culture

Concepts such as the unconscious, defence mechanisms, slips of the tongue and transference are part of everyday language. Scientific psychology has confirmed that much mental processing is unconscious, but in a different sense from Freud's: automatic, not repressed.

Defence mechanisms

One of the psychoanalytic ideas that has best stood the test of time is that we protect ourselves from distress with manoeuvres that are not always conscious. Anna Freud systematised them in 1936 in The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence: repression, denial, projection, rationalisation, displacement and others. The psychiatrist George Vaillant ranked them from most immature to most mature, such as humour, sublimation and anticipation, and in Harvard's Grant Study found that people who used mature defences had better health and relationships throughout life.

Can it be refuted?

The philosopher Karl Popper used psychoanalysis as an example of an unscientific theory: any behaviour could be explained after the fact, and if a patient rejected an interpretation, that was taken as proof of resistance. Adolf Grünbaum replied in 1984 that some Freudian claims were testable, but that the clinical evidence they rested on was contaminated by the analyst's suggestion. This debate pushed psychoanalysts to do research with more rigorous methods, such as clinical trials and studies of therapeutic process.

Bowlby, a critical son

John Bowlby trained as a psychoanalyst in London but gradually moved away from orthodoxy. He thought that what mattered in childhood was not the child's fantasies but what actually happened in their relationship with carers, and he sought support in ethology and direct observation. Attachment theory, today one of the best supported in developmental psychology, grew out of that turn. For years, official psychoanalysis received it coldly.

Argentina, capital of psychoanalysis

Argentina is probably the country with the most psychologists per inhabitant in the world, and psychoanalysis has an enormous cultural presence there, in universities, clinics and everyday life. Buenos Aires even has a neighbourhood nicknamed "Villa Freud". The reasons are several: the arrival of European psychoanalysts fleeing Nazism, the influence of Jacques Lacan from the 1960s and an urban society very open to talking about psychological matters.

A school's historical importance and the current scientific support for its ideas are different things: we explain them separately.
